title: Stay with the Lord, my mind
hookLine: ae man meriaa too sadaa rahu har naale: stay always with the Lord and your troubles will pass (Anand 2)

lines: THE GURU TALKS TO HIS OWN MIND.
cards: Come on. Focus. Don't check the phone.
You've got this. Plenty of people talk to themselves, even if they'd never admit it. Some of it is harsh, the inner voice that sounds like a bad coach.

Some is kinder. Either way, the mind needs reminding, again and again, of what it already knows, because it wanders off the moment you stop watching. The second pauri of Anand Sahib is the Guru talking to his own mind.
Not to a crowd. Not even to God, exactly. To himself.

teach.h: AE MAN MERIAA: O MY MIND.
teach.b: The pauri opens, transliterated: ae man meriaa too sadaa rahu har naale. O my mind, always stay with the Lord. Man is the mind, the restless inner self.
Meriaa: my. Sadaa: always. Har naale: with the Lord, alongside.

Then, in paraphrase: stay with the Lord, my mind, and all your pains will be forgotten. He will take you as his own, and set all your affairs right. The Master can do all things; why forget him from your mind?
And it ends where it began: says Nanak, my mind, always stay with the Lord. Listen to the tone. It's not scolding.
It's someone who has just found joy in pauri one, turning to his wandering mind and saying: stay. Don't drift off now.
Naale is a lovely little word: beside, alongside, the word for walking with a friend. Not under, not far above. With.
The promise is about the pains being forgotten, not about them never happening. The troubles are real; in the pauri, staying beside the Lord is what loosens their grip.
Angeekaar, being taken as his own, is the idea you met in Chaupai: claimed, held, adopted.

teach.h: WHY FORGET HIM? NOT A THREAT.
teach.b: And then that gentle question, why forget him? Not a threat. Almost puzzled, the way you'd ask a friend who keeps wandering off from the one person who always shows up for them.
Now the work is to stay with it.

how: Many Sikhs recite this second pauri as part of the short Anand Sahib sung at the close of services, and the opening line is often quoted as a reminder to keep the mind with God through the day.

s: pauri two is addressed to a crowd
ae man meriaa: it's addressed to the Guru's own mind.
the pauri says staying with the Lord means troubles never happen
it says the pains will be forgotten, their grip loosened, not that they never come.
naale means alongside, the way you'd walk with a friend
not under or far above: with.

games.q: you've just found joy, and already your mind is wandering off to the next worry. what does pauri two say to it?
o: scold it harshly until it obeys.
O my mind, always stay with the Lord.
let it wander; it doesn't matter.
games.why: ae man meriaa too sadaa rahu har naale: O my mind, always stay with the Lord. said gently, with a puzzled question: why forget him?

practice: Choose one simple thing to stay with: your breath, the sound of a fan, or Waheguru if you pray. Every time the mind wanders off, and it will, bring it back gently, the way the pauri does, with no scolding: just, stay.

wordCard.voice: Man meriaa, O my mind. Ae man meriaa too sadaa rahu har naale: the Guru telling his own mind, gently, to stay beside the Lord, and the pains will loosen.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: man meriaa, O my mind, the address that opens Anand Sahib's second pauri.

carryVoice: Your line: stay with him. The mind wanders; the pauri keeps calling it back, kindly. Until tomorrow, then.
